strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical limitation of learned sparse-view CT reconstruction: models tied to a fixed number of views and image resolution. A unified model that works across acquisition rates would be valuable for deployment.

The proposed CTO architecture is technically coherent: it combines unrolled reconstruction, data consistency, sinogram-domain processing, image-domain processing, DISCO neural-operator layers, and a physically motivated flipped circular padding scheme for sinogram angular periodicity.

Empirical results are promising. On two CT datasets, CTO reports consistent improvements over FBP, SART, unrolled CNN, DuDoTrans, GloReDi, and diffusion baselines, with sizeable PSNR/RMSE/SSIM gains across 18/36/72-view settings.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses, including sinogram frequency-domain variants, rotational equivariance padding, inference-time comparison to diffusion baselines, and zero-shot super-resolution probes for both image and sinogram resolutions.
The method has a plausible efficiency advantage over diffusion-based posterior sampling, with reported single-pass inference around 0.065s versus tens of seconds for DPS/ALD on an A100.
weaknesses: The central resolution- and sampling-agnostic claim is only partially demonstrated. For sparse-view rates, the main setup trains a single model jointly over all evaluated sampling rates, so the evidence is more multi-rate interpolation/conditioning than true generalization to unseen acquisition settings. It is unclear how CTO behaves on view counts, angular patterns, detector sizes, or geometries not observed in training.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The work appears to adapt DISCO/UDNO neural operators and ideas from resolution-agnostic MRI/computational imaging to CT, with sensible sinogram-domain modifications. The paper would benefit from a sharper distinction between what is new algorithmically and what is inherited from prior neural-operator imaging work.

The evaluation relies on simulated sinograms generated from image datasets rather than real raw projection data with realistic scanner physics, dose-dependent noise, beam hardening, scatter, calibration effects, or clinical reconstruction protocols. This weakens the deployment-oriented claims.

Some comparisons may not be fully conclusive. Diffusion baselines are evaluated on a subset due to cost and are reportedly trained for only 2,000 iterations, which may understate their performance. It is also unclear whether all learned baselines are equally optimized for the multi-rate setting, and comparisons to per-rate specialist models are not sufficiently emphasized.

The zero-shot super-resolution experiments are limited. The image-resolution test compares against bilinearly interpolated 512x512 ground truth, and the setup involves upsampling intermediate reconstructions before applying the image operator, so it does not fully establish clinically meaningful high-resolution reconstruction from genuinely higher-resolution measurements.

The theoretical treatment of equivariance is convincing for ideal parallel-beam geometry, but the experiments also include fan-beam AAPM settings. The paper does not clearly explain how the stated sinogram symmetries and padding assumptions transfer to fan-beam geometry.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places: hyperparameter tuning is summarized but not exhaustive, code availability is not stated, exact training schedules for all baselines are unevenly specified, and some claims such as 'tuning required' are qualitative.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: sparse-view CT models that can operate across different view counts and image resolutions without maintaining a separate model per acquisition setting.

The architectural idea of combining unrolled reconstruction, sinogram-domain processing, image-domain refinement, DISCO/neural-operator layers, and CT-specific angular padding is plausible and reasonably motivated by CT geometry.

The reported quantitative gains over CNN, transformer, diffusion, SART, and FBP baselines are large on two datasets, and the paper includes ablations for frequency-domain sinogram learning and circular padding.
The manuscript is generally readable and gives enough high-level architectural detail to understand the intended design.
weaknesses: The central claim of resolution- and sampling-rate generalization is not convincingly tested. The main multi-rate experiment trains a single model jointly on the evaluated sampling rates, so it demonstrates interpolation over trained acquisition settings rather than zero-shot generalization to unseen sampling rates. The only zero-shot tests are narrow and mostly qualitative.

The experimental protocol raises fairness concerns. Diffusion baselines are reportedly trained for only 2,000 iterations despite using a 65M-parameter model, evaluated on only a 500-slice subset for the kidney dataset, and omitted from the larger full-test comparison. This makes the strong speed/quality claims versus diffusion insufficiently supported.

The theory/geometry claims are overstated. The rotation-equivariance derivation applies cleanly to parallel-beam CT with pi-periodicity, but the paper also evaluates AAPM with fan-beam geometry and [0, 2pi) sampling without explaining how the same symmetry, padding, and operator formulation remain valid. The empirical equivariance evidence is a small padding ablation, not a rigorous equivariance/generalization test.

The cross-resolution experiment is weak: high-resolution ground truth is described as bilinearly interpolated 512x512 images rather than genuinely higher-resolution data, and results are shown mainly through a figure with very limited numerical detail. This does not substantiate clinical or physical super-resolution capability.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior DISCO/UDNO neural-operator work for computational imaging, especially the cited compressed-sensing MRI model. The paper largely transfers that template to CT with sinogram-domain processing, but does not clearly separate new algorithmic content from reused neural-operator machinery.

Implementation details are incomplete or internally limiting for a resolution-independent method. For example, DISCO kernels are said to be defined over an input domain of size 256x256, while the method claims arbitrary image resolution; the data-consistency module, forward operators, normalization, HU conversion, and handling of fan-beam geometry are under-specified.

The paper lacks important medical-imaging validation: no robustness to noise, dose level, scanner/protocol shift, pathology-level analysis, uncertainty, reader study, or out-of-distribution acquisition test. Given the deployment-oriented claims, the evidence remains too narrow.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, hyperparameter tuning is vaguely described, and several baselines rely on unspecified adaptations to the multi-rate setting. Some presentation issues also remain, including typographical errors and unclear figure/table references.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical limitation of learned sparse-view CT reconstruction: models tied to a fixed view count and image resolution. Framing both sinograms and images as functions and using neural operators is well matched to this problem.

The proposed CTO design is technically coherent. The combination of an unrolled data-consistency architecture, a sinogram-space DISCO operator, an image-space DISCO operator, detector-axis frequency processing, and flipped circular angular padding is motivated by CT geometry rather than being a generic architecture swap.

Empirical results are strong across two CT datasets. CTO consistently improves over FBP, SART, unrolled CNN, DuDoTrans, GloReDi, and diffusion baselines, with large PSNR/RMSE/SSIM gains on both kidney and abdominal low-dose CT settings.
The efficiency comparison is compelling: CTO is reported as single-pass and much faster than diffusion posterior sampling or ALD, which is highly relevant for clinical deployment.

The ablations support several core design choices, including rotation-equivariant padding and frequency-domain sinogram processing. The zero-shot image and sinogram super-resolution experiments are also useful evidence for the claimed resolution-agnostic behavior.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with helpful architectural diagrams, implementation details, and supplementary tables on full test-set evaluation.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental rather than foundational: much of the machinery comes from prior DISCO/UDNO neural operators and unrolled reconstruction networks. The main contribution is a well-engineered adaptation to CT with sinogram-domain design, which is valuable but not a major conceptual breakthrough.

The central claim of generalization across sampling rates is somewhat weakened because the main multi-rate experiments train a single model jointly on the evaluated view counts. This demonstrates one model covering multiple rates, but it is less convincing as evidence of true out-of-distribution sampling-rate generalization.

The zero-shot super-resolution experiments are promising but limited. Ground truth is described as bilinearly interpolated in the 512x512 case, and comparisons are mainly against a CNN baseline, so the evidence for high-resolution clinical reconstruction is not yet fully satisfying.

The diffusion baseline may be disadvantaged or insufficiently documented: it is trained for only 2,000 iterations, evaluated on a subset for some comparisons due to cost, and may require stronger tuning or more recent CT-specific diffusion baselines to make the reported margins fully conclusive.

The evaluation uses simulated sparse-view measurements generated from image datasets rather than raw projection data, and clinical realism is therefore limited. More evidence under scanner-specific noise, beam hardening, fan/cone-beam geometry, and domain shifts would strengthen the deployment claims.

The rotation-equivariance discussion is strongest for parallel-beam geometry, while one evaluated dataset uses fan-beam settings. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of which symmetry assumptions still hold under fan-beam acquisition and whether the same padding/equivariance argument remains exact or approximate.

Reproducibility is moderate but not complete: many implementation details are given, but the paper does not clearly state code/data release plans, parameter counts for all baselines, training budgets for every method, or statistical significance testing.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: a single sparse-view CT reconstruction model that can handle multiple sampling rates and resolutions is practically important, and the paper clearly explains why fixed-rate CNN/unrolled models are limiting.

The proposed CTO combines several sensible design choices: neural-operator/DISCO layers for discretization robustness, dual-domain sinogram and image processing, detector-axis Fourier processing motivated by FBP/Fourier slice structure, and angular padding to encode tomographic rotational structure.

Empirical results are broad and mostly strong. The paper reports consistent gains over classical, unrolled, transformer, CNN, and diffusion baselines on AAPM and Kidney CT, with additional LIDC-IDRI results, noisy-sinogram and cross-dataset checks, zero-shot resolution experiments, runtime comparisons, and ablations of NO_s, NO_i, circular padding, and frequency branches.

The runtime story is attractive: CTO is reported to be substantially faster than diffusion posterior methods while achieving better PSNR/SSIM, and the complexity analysis argues that DISCO has little or no inference overhead relative to comparable convolutions once kernels are discretized.

The manuscript is generally clear and gives useful implementation details, including dataset splits, sampling settings, baseline descriptions, training hardware, kernel hyperparameter analysis, and supplementary quantitative tables.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that the gains come from neural-operator/function-space modeling is not fully isolated. The Unrolled CNN baseline is described in the main text as CTO with DISCO replaced by regular convolutions, but the supplementary baseline description says it operates entirely in image space and does not apply learned sinogram processing. This makes the main comparison potentially confound neural operators with the addition of a dual-domain sinogram module.

The resolution-agnostic claim is broader than the evidence. Most main experiments use fixed simulated geometries and fixed 256x256 image resolution, while the zero-shot super-resolution evaluation compares against bilinearly upsampled ground truth rather than native high-resolution acquisitions. This supports interpolation/discretization robustness, but not yet arbitrary clinical resolution or scanner generalization.

The tomography physics assumptions are somewhat under-examined. The rotation-equivariant derivation is natural for parallel-beam CT, but the paper also evaluates fan-beam AAPM data with 0 to 2pi angles; it is not fully clear that the flipped circular padding and claimed SO(2)-equivariance apply cleanly there or under arbitrary sparse sampling masks.

The clinical realism is limited. Sparse-view sinograms appear to be generated from reconstructed CT images rather than raw measured projection data, and the experiments do not cover cone-beam/helical 3D CT, scanner-specific calibration effects, metal, motion, realistic dose/noise variation beyond one Poisson-noise test, or reader/diagnostic downstream evaluation.

Some comparisons may be imperfectly tuned or not fully balanced. The diffusion baseline is trained for only 2,000 iterations despite using a 65M-parameter model, runtime comparisons include only selected methods, and several strong recent CT reconstruction methods are discussed but not always included in the quantitative tables.

Reproducibility is weakened by small but important omissions: the abstract says code is available but the URL is blank, and some architectural details are inconsistent across sections. The paper is detailed overall, but these inconsistencies matter because the claimed contribution depends on fair architectural attribution.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: a single sparse-view CT reconstruction model that can handle multiple view counts and image/sinogram resolutions without retraining.

The proposed system combines sensible ingredients: dual-domain sinogram/image processing, unrolled data consistency, DISCO/UDNO neural-operator layers, and sinogram-domain frequency processing motivated by CT reconstruction physics.

The manuscript reports extensive empirical results across AAPM, KiTS, and LIDC-IDRI, with multiple baselines, ablations for NOs/NOi and frequency branches, runtime comparisons, and some OOD/noisy-sinogram tests.
The reported gains over the matched unrolled CNN baseline are substantial, suggesting that continuous/local operator parameterization may be useful for CT reconstruction under multi-rate training.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly presents CTO as inherently resolution- and sampling-rate agnostic, but the main experiments largely use multi-rate co-training over a fixed set of rates rather than convincing zero-shot generalization to arbitrary acquisition settings. This weakens the main scientific claim.

There is a serious mismatch between the theoretical rotation-equivariance argument and the experimental setup. The derivation assumes parallel-beam CT and pi-periodicity with detector flip, while the main AAPM setup uses fan-beam geometry over 0 to 2pi. The paper does not adequately justify that the claimed equivariance or padding rule applies to the primary benchmark.

The comparison to diffusion baselines appears potentially unfair: the supplement states that a 65M-parameter diffusion model is trained for only 2,000 iterations, yet the paper makes strong claims of outperforming state-of-the-art diffusion methods by large margins and being 500x faster. Runtime superiority is expected, but reconstruction-quality comparisons need stronger baseline training and validation.

The zero-shot super-resolution evidence is not fully convincing. For image-space super-resolution, the ground truth is a bilinearly interpolated 512x512 target and the intermediate reconstruction is also upsampled, so the experiment does not demonstrate recovery of true high-resolution CT content. For sinogram super-resolution, the paper reports only summarized gains without enough protocol detail to establish clinical relevance.

The evaluation relies on simulated sparse-view sinograms generated from reconstructed CT images rather than real sparse acquisition data. This is common in the area, but the manuscript makes broad clinical-practice claims without scanner/protocol diversity, radiologist evaluation, uncertainty analysis, or 3D validation.

The novelty is incremental: much of the architecture is a combination of known unrolled reconstruction, dual-domain processing, and existing DISCO/UDNO neural operators. The paper’s strongest contribution is an application/adaptation to CT, but the presentation frames it as a broader foundational advance.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available, but the link is blank in the manuscript. Several baseline details and hyperparameter choices are in the supplement, but the fairness of tuning across methods remains difficult to verify.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations/societal-impact discussion despite medical-imaging claims. Important limitations such as synthetic sinograms, fan-beam versus parallel-beam theory, 2D-only evaluation, and clinical deployment risks are only briefly or indirectly acknowledged.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: sparse-view CT models that are brittle to changing view counts and resolutions. The proposed CTO framework is well motivated as an Algorithms/General contribution, combining unrolled reconstruction, neural operators, sinogram/image-domain processing, and CT-specific rotational structure.

The empirical evidence is broad and generally convincing. CTO improves over learning-free methods, unrolled CNN/transformer baselines, dual-domain methods, and diffusion baselines on AAPM and Kidney CT, with sizeable gains in PSNR/RMSE/SSIM across 18/36/72-view settings and additional 9-view, LIDC-IDRI, cross-dataset, and noisy-sinogram results.

The paper includes useful ablations: sinogram vs image operators, spatial vs frequency sinogram branches, circular padding/rotation-equivariance, FFT variants, single-rate vs multi-rate training, and complexity/runtime comparisons. These support the main design choices rather than only reporting benchmark wins.

The resolution-agnostic and multi-rate framing is a meaningful contribution for CT reconstruction. The zero-shot image/sinogram super-resolution experiments are particularly aligned with the neural-operator claim and distinguish the method from standard CNN reconstruction pipelines.

The manuscript is mostly clear, with a coherent connection between CT physics, Fourier slice motivation, function-space operators, and unrolled data consistency. The appendix gives substantial implementation detail for datasets, baselines, hyperparameters, and computational cost.
weaknesses: Some central claims are somewhat overstated. The discretization convergence and rotation-equivariance arguments are largely inherited from DISCO or shown under idealized assumptions; the full CTO pipeline, learned unrolling, data-consistency steps, finite discretization, and fan-beam geometry are not rigorously shown to preserve these properties.

The evaluation appears to rely on generated sinograms from CT images rather than raw scanner projection measurements, and realistic clinical acquisition effects are only lightly addressed through simulated Poisson noise. This limits the strength of claims about clinical protocol variability and real-world robustness.

The comparison to baselines is strong but not fully clean. The unrolled CNN baseline is described as image-domain only, while CTO has both sinogram and image operators, so the main CNN-vs-NO comparison partly conflates function-space kernels with dual-domain architecture. A matched dual-domain CNN with the same sinogram/image structure would make the case sharper.

The diffusion baseline may be under-optimized or not representative of the strongest published diffusion CT systems, since it is trained for only 2,000 iterations and uses a fixed 1,000-step posterior-sampling setup. The speed comparison is still useful, but the accuracy comparison should be interpreted cautiously.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says code is available but the URL is blank, and several implementation details that matter for CT geometry, operator discretization, and data preprocessing would need released code to verify. This is a notable weakness for a complex reconstruction pipeline.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit limitations section. It mentions future work on clinically relevant datasets, 3D CT, uncertainty, and broader protocols, but these are important constraints on the current claims rather than merely future extensions.
